<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in Cook's equational theory $\PV$ (a polynomial-time equational theory). The base sort is finite Boolean strings $\zo^* = \{0,1\}^*$ with constant $\eps$ (empty string), unary successors $s_0, s_1$ (append a 0 or a 1 to the right), binary concatenation $\circ$, smash $\#$, trim-right $\TR$, and iterated trim $\ITR$. The defining axioms are $x \circ \eps = x$, $x \circ s_i(y) = s_i(x \circ y)$, $\TR(\eps) = \eps$, $\TR(s_i(x)) = x$, $\ITR(x, \eps) = x$, $\ITR(x, s_i(y)) = \TR(\ITR(x, y))$, $x \# \eps = \eps$, $x \# s_i(y) = x \circ (x \# y)$ ($i \in \{0,1\}$). New functions are introduced by composition or by limited recursion on notation, the latter requiring an order-$(i-1)$ $\PV$ proof of $\ITR(h_i(\vec x, y, z), z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)) = \eps$. Equations are derived using (L0) reflexivity, (L1) symmetry, (L2) transitivity, (L3) congruence, (L4) substitution, the definition axioms, and the structural-induction rule: from $f_j(\vec x, \eps) = g(\vec x)$ and $f_j(\vec x, s_i(y)) = h_i(\vec x, y, f_j(\vec x, y))$ ($i \in \{0,1\}$, $j \in \{1,2\}$) infer $f_1(\vec x, y) = f_2(\vec x, y)$. The standard model is denoted $\M$; $t^\M$ is the interpretation of term $t$ in $\M$. $\FP$ is the class of polynomial-time computable functions. $\calF, \calF'$ are Cobham's class and its variant (with the modified bound $|h_i(\vec x, y, z)| \le |z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)|$).

Lemma (book label `lmm: Fp subset F`).

Let $\calF'$ be the class obtained by replacing the inequalities $h_i(\vec x,y)\le k(\vec x,y)$ in the rule of limited induction on notation in $\calF$ to $|h_i(\vec x,y,z)|\le|z\circ k_i(\vec x,y)|$ for $i\in\zo$. Then $\calF'\subseteq\calF$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We first show that $\calF'\subseteq\calF$ by structural induction over the Cobham rules (with the updated limited recursion on notation rule). We need to prove that if $f$ is introduced from $g,h_1,h_2\in\calF$ by the limited recursion on notation rule of Cobham's class such that $|h_i(\vec x,y,z)|\le|z\circ k_i(\vec x,y,z)|$ for some $k_i\in\calF$, $i\in\zo$, then $f\in\calF$. Indeed, we will prove $f\in\FP$ and apply Cobham's theorem (see Cobham's theorem (1965): $\calF = \FP$). This follows from the fact that  
    \begin{align*}
    |f(\vec x,s_i(y))| &\le |h_i(\vec x,y,f(\vec x,y))|\\ 
    &\le |f(\vec x,y)| + |k_i(\vec x,y)| \tag{unfolding $f$ recursively}\\
    &\le |g(\vec x)| + \sum_{0\le j< |s_i(y)|} |k_{\BIT(s_i(y),j+1)}(\vec x,s_i(y)_{>j}))| \le \poly(|\vec x|,|y|)
    \end{align*}
    and that $g,h_0,h_1\in\calF=\FP$. (Notice that the the computation of $f$ only requires calling $g,h_0,h_1$ on inputs of $\poly(|\vec x|,|y|)$ length.)
</informal_proof>

The standard model is denoted $\M$; $t^\M$ is the interpretation of term $t$ in $\M$. $\FP$ is the class of polynomial-time computable functions. $\calF, \calF'$ are Cobham's class and its variant (with the modified bound $|h_i(\vec x, y, z)| \le |z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)|$).

Proposition (book label `prop: empty left`).

$\PV\vdash \eps \circ x = x$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We define two $\PV$ functions $f_1(x) \eqdef \eps\circ x$ and $f_2(x) \eqdef x$ by the composition rule using terms $\eps\circ x$ and $x$, respectively. We will prove in $\PV$ that $f_1(x)=f_2(x)$, which immediately implies $\eps\circ x=x$ by (L2) transitivity and the definition axioms of $f_1$ and $f_2$. 

Intuitively, the proof follows from a structural induction on $x$. We first verify the base case, i.e., $x=\eps$: 
\begin{align*}
    \PV&\vdash f_1(\eps)  = \eps \circ \eps \tag{(L4) substitution $x/\eps$ to the definition axiom} \\ 
    \PV&\vdash x\circ\eps = x \tag{the defining axiom of concatenation: $x \circ \eps = x$ and $x \circ s_i(y) = s_i(x \circ y)$ for $i \in \{0,1\}$} \\ 
    \PV&\vdash \eps\circ\eps=\eps \tag{(L4) substitution $x/\eps$ to the equation above} \\ 
    \PV&\vdash f_1(\eps) = \eps \tag{(L2) transitivity}
\end{align*}
Similarly, $f_2(\eps) = \eps$. Therefore, let $g = \eps$ be a function with no variable, then $f_j(\eps) = g$ ($j\in\{1,2\}$) is provable in $\PV$.  

Then, we consider the induction step, i.e., $x$ is of the form $s_i(x)$ for $i\in\zo$. Notice that for every $i\in\zo$:  
\begin{align*}
\PV & \vdash f_1(s_i(x)) = \eps \circ s_i(x)  \tag{(L4) substitution $x/s_i(x)$ to the definition axiom} \\ 
\PV & \vdash \eps \circ s_i(x) = s_i(\eps\circ x)\;  \tag{(L4) substitution $x/\eps,y/x$ to the defining axiom of concatenation: $x \circ \eps = x$ and $x \circ s_i(y) = s_i(x \circ y)$ for $i \in \{0,1\}$} \\ 
(*) \; \PV & \vdash \eps\circ x = f_1(x) \tag{(L1) symmetricity to the definition axiom} \\ 
(\star) \; \PV & \vdash s_i(x) = s_i(x) \tag{(L0) reflexivity} \\ 
\PV & \vdash s_i(\eps\circ x) = s_i(f_1(x)) \tag{(L3) substitution with ($\star$) and ($*$)} \\ 
\PV & \vdash f_1(s_i(x)) = s_i(f_1(x)) \tag{(L2) transitivity} 
\end{align*}
Similarly, one can prove that $f_2(s_i(x)) = s_i(f_2(x))$. Therefore, let $h_i(x,z) = s_i(z)$, we can prove that for $j\in\{1,2\}$ and $i\in\zo$: 
\[
\PV\vdash f_j(s_i(x)) = h_i(x,f_j(x)).
\]
Then, by the rule of structural induction, we can prove that $f_1(x) = f_2(x)$ as they are both inductively defined from $(g,h_0,h_1)$.
</informal_proof>

Proposition (book label `prop: circ assoc`).

$\PV\vdash (x\circ y)\circ z = x\circ (y\circ z)$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We define two functions $f_1(x,y,z) \eqdef (x\circ y)\circ z$ and $f_2(x,y,z) \eqdef x\circ (y\circ z)$, and it suffices to prove that $f_1(x,y,z)=f_2(x,y,z)$. The strategy is to use the induction rule. Notice that
    \begin{align*}
    \PV\vdash& f_1(x,y,\eps) = (x\circ y)\circ \eps \tag{(L4) substitution $z/\eps$ to the definition axiom} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& x\circ \eps = x \tag{Definition axiom of $\circ$} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& (x\circ y)\circ \eps = x\circ y \tag{(L4) substitution $x/(x\circ y)$ to equation above} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& f_1(x,y,\eps) = x\circ y\tag{(L2) transitivity}
    \end{align*}
    Similarly, we can (with slightly more steps) prove that $\PV\vdash f_2(x,y,\eps) = x\circ y$. 

    Also, notice that for every $i\in\zo$, 
    \begin{align*}
    \PV\vdash& f_1(x,y,s_i(z)) = (x\circ y)\circ s_i(z) \tag{(L4) substitution to the definition axiom} \\
    \PV\vdash& x\circ s_i(y') = s_i(x\circ y') \tag{Definition axiom of $\circ$}\\ 
    \PV\vdash& (x\circ y)\circ s_i(z) = s_i((x\circ y)\circ z) \tag{(L4) substitution $x/(x\circ y)$ and $y'/z$} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& (x\circ y)\circ z = f_1(x,y,z) \tag{(L1) symmetricity to the definition axiom} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& s_i((x\circ y)\circ z) = s_i(f_1(x,y,z)) \tag{(L3) using above and function $s_i$} \\ 
    \PV\vdash& f_1(x,y,s_i(z)) = s_i(f_1(x,y,z)) \tag{(L2) transitivity, twice}
    \end{align*}
    Similarly, we can (again with slightly more steps) prove that $\PV\vdash f_2(x,y,s_i(z)) = s_i(f_2(x,y,z))$. Therefore, by the induction rule using $g(x,y)\eqdef x\circ y$ and $h_i(x,y,z) = s_i(z)$, we can prove that $f_1(x,y,z) = f_2(x,y,z)$.
</informal_proof>

Lemma (book label `lmm: soundness`).

The following two properties hold. 
\begin{compactitem}
    \item For every $\PV$ function $f$, its standard interpretation $f^\M\in\calF'$. 
    \item $\PV$ satisfies its standard model. 
\end{compactitem}
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We prove by simultaneous induction on $k$ that (1) every $k$-order $\PV$ function is interpreted as a polynomial-time computable function by $\calI_k^\ff$ and (2) every order-$k$ provable equation $e:s=t$ satisfies that $s^{\calI_k^\cn,\calI_k^\ff}$ and $t^{\calI_k^\cn,\calI_k^\ff}$ are the same function. The base case for $k=0$ is obvious. For $k\ge 1$, we can see that: 
\begin{itemize}
\item For any function $f=f_t^{(0)}$ introduced by the composition rule, we know by the induction hypothesis that all order-$(k-1)$ functions are interpreted as functions in $\calF'$ (by $\calI_k^\ff$), and thus all order-$(k-1)$ terms are interpreted as functions in $\calF'$. It follows by the definition of $\calI^\ff_k$ that $f^{\calI^\ff_k}\in\calF'$. 
\item For any function $f=f^{(1)}_\Pi$ introduced by the recursion rule, where the tuple $\Pi=(g,h_0,h_1,k_0,k_1,\pi_0,\pi_1)$, $\pi_0,\pi_1$ are order-$(k-1)$ proofs of the inequality $\ITR(h_i(\vec x, y, z), z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)) = \eps$ for $i \in \{0,1\}$, and $g,h_0,h_1,k_0,k_1\in\calF'$. By the definition of the inequality $\ITR(h_i(\vec x, y, z), z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)) = \eps$ for $i \in \{0,1\}$, its standard interpretation, and the induction hypothesis (2), we know that over the standard model $\M$, 
\[
|h_i^\M(\vec x,y,z)|\le|z\circ k_i^\M(\vec x,y)|\quad i\in\zo

and thus $f^\M\in\calF'$.

Theorem (book label `thm: case study`).

Let $s(\vec x,y) = t(\vec x, y)$ be an equation. If 
\begin{compactitem}
\item $\PV\vdash s(\vec x,\eps) = t(\vec x,\eps)$; 
\item $\PV\vdash s(\vec x, s_i(y)) = t(\vec x,s_i(y))$ for $i\in\zo$;

then $\PV\vdash s(\vec x,y) = t(\vec x, y)$.

    \begin{align*}
    g(\vec x) &\eqdef f_s(\vec x,\eps) \\

    \PV &\vdash f_t(\vec x,\eps) = g(\vec x) \\

Theorem ($\PV$ as a PPS) (book label `thm: pv pps`).

Let $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ be propositional formulas consisting of variables and constants (i.e.~\texttt{True} or \texttt{False}), and $\pb_{\varphi_1},\pb_{\varphi_2}$ be the $\PV$-terms by replacing propositional connectives with $\{\And,\Or,\Not\}$ and replacing \texttt{True} and \texttt{False} with $s_1(t)$ and $s_0(t')$ for arbitrary terms $t$ and $t'$ (not necessarily the same for all replacements). Assume that there is no variable that appears in exactly one of $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$. Then: $\varphi_1\equiv \varphi_2$ if and only if $\PV\vdash \LastBit(\pb_{\varphi_1}) = \LastBit(\pb_{\varphi_2})$.
</informal_theorem>

By the interpretation of $\ITE$ in $\M$, we can see that it immediately implies that for all assignments to variables $\vec x\in\{\texttt{True},\texttt{False}\}^*$, $\varphi_1(\vec x) = \varphi_2(\vec x)$, which implies that $\varphi_1\equiv \varphi_2$. Now we prove the other side. Let $k\in\N$ be the number of variables involved in $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$. We prove that there is a $\PV$-proof of $\pb_{\varphi_1}=\pb_{\varphi_2}$ for every $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ such that $\varphi_1\equiv\varphi_2$ by induction on $k$. (Note that this induction is not made within $\PV$ but in our meta-theory.) The case for $k=0$ is simple: By referring to the axioms of $\ITE$ (see the defining axioms of $\ITE$: $\ITE(s_0(x), u, v) = v$ and $\ITE(s_1(x), u, v) = u$) and using the logical rules for equation (as well as using the meta-theorem the theorem allowing case analysis via $\ITE$), we can prove in $\PV$ for some $b\in\zo$ that $\LastBit(\pb_{\varphi_1}) = b$ and $\LastBit(\pb_{\varphi_2})=b$, i.e., we can evaluate both sides of the equation. Let $\pb_{\varphi_1'}(\vec x,y)$ and $\pb_{\varphi_2'}(\vec x,y)$ be the terms embedding $\varphi_1'$ and $\varphi_2'$ into $\PV$ as mentioned above, respectively. \begin{compactitem}
\item replacing propositional connectives with $\{\And,\Or,\Not\}$,
\item replacing \texttt{True} and \texttt{False} with $s_1(t)$ and $s_0(t')$ for arbitrary terms $t,t'$. 
\end{compactitem}

Notice that as $\varphi_1'\equiv\varphi_2'$, we know that $\varphi_1'(\vec x,y/i)\equiv \varphi_2'(\vec x,y/i)$ for $i\in\zo$. Therefore, by the induction hypothesis, there are $\PV$-proofs of 
\begin{equation}
\LastBit(p_{\varphi'_1}(\vec x,s_i(w))) = \LastBit(p_{\varphi'_2}(\vec x,s_i(w))) \label{equ: tech prop ind}
\end{equation}
for $i\in\zo$. Also, we can prove (by the equation $\ITE(\eps, u, v) = \eps$ and the last-bit-of-string equation used in the if-then-else case study) that 
\begin{equation}
\LastBit(p_{\varphi'_1}(\vec x,\eps)) = \LastBit(p_{\varphi'_2}(\vec x,\eps));\label{equ: tech prop base}
\end{equation}
indeed, $\PV$ proves that both sides of the equation are equal to $\eps$ (recall that $y$ appears in both $\varphi'_1$ and $\varphi'_2$). We can then prove 
\begin{equation}
\LastBit(p_{\varphi'_1}(\vec x,y)) = \LastBit(p_{\varphi'_2}(\vec x,y))
\end{equation}
by applying the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable) (i.e.~proof by case study) on $y$.

Lemma (book label `lmm: pair correctness`).

$\PV$ proves the following equations: 
\begin{compactitem}
\item $\Left(\MakePair(x,y)) = x$;
\item $\Right(\MakePair(x,y)) = y$. 
\end{compactitem}
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
(\emph{Correctness of $\Right$}). We start by proving the second equation. We first need to prove that: 
\begin{equation}
\RightRaw(\MakePair(x,y)) = \ITE^{(\eps)}_0(\FirstBit(y),\PEnc(y),1\circ\PEnc(y))\label{equ: right raw}
\end{equation}
where $\FirstBit(y)\eqdef \ITR(y,\TR(y))$, $\ITE^{(\eps)}_0(c,x,y)$ outputs $y$ if $c=\eps$ or $\LastBit(c)=1$, and outputs $x$ if $\LastBit(c)=0$. This equation formally describes the fact that 
\[ 
\RightRaw(\MakePair(x,y))
\] 
is $1\circ \PEnc(y)$ if $y=\eps$ or the leftmost bit of $y$ is $0$, and is $\PEnc(y)$ otherwise. the equation `equ: right raw` can be proved by induction on $y$ that both sides of the equation are identical to the function recursively defined by $g(x)=1$ and 
\begin{align}
h_0(x,y,z) &= \ITE(\IsEps(y),100,s_0(s_0(z))) \\ 
h_1(x,y,z) &= \ITE(\IsEps(y),10,s_0(s_1(z)))
\end{align}
for $i\in\zo$. Note that 
\begin{itemize}
\item To prove that the LHS of the equation `equ: right raw` is equal to the function recursively defined by $g,h_0,h_1$, notice that $\PV$ proves 
\[ 
\RightRaw(\MakePair(x,s_i(y)))=s_0(\RightRaw(s_i(\MakePair(x,y))))
\] 
by unfolding for $i\in\zo$. Then we prove by a case study on $y$ that 
\begin{align*}
\PV\vdash&~s_0(\RightRaw(s_0(\MakePair(x,y)))) = \ITE(\IsEps(y),100,s_0(s_0(z)) )\\ 
\PV\vdash&~s_0(\RightRaw(s_1(\MakePair(x,y)))) = \ITE(\IsEps(y),10,s_0(s_0(z)) )
\end{align*}
by the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable). Notice that the RHS of the equations above are exactly $h_0(x,y,z)$ and $h_1(x,y,z)$. 
\item To prove that the RHS of the equation `equ: right raw` is equal to the function recursively defined by $g,h_0,h_1$, the hard part is to prove that $\PV$ proves 
\begin{align*}
& \ITE^{(\eps)}_0(\FirstBit(s_i(y)),\PEnc(s_i(y)),1\circ\PEnc(s_i(y))) \\ 
= & h_i(x,y,\ITE^{(\eps)}_0(\FirstBit(y),\PEnc(y),1\circ\PEnc(y))) 
\end{align*}
for $i\in\zo$. We can prove this by case study on $y$ using the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable), the fact that $\PV\vdash\FirstBit(s_j(s_i(y))) = \FirstBit(s_i(y))$, and a strengthened form of the if-then-else case theorem. 
\end{itemize}
The details of the proofs above are omitted. 

Now we prove that $\Right(\MakePair(x,y)) = y$. Notice that $\PV$ proves the following sequence of calculation: 
\begin{align}
    &~\Right(\MakePair(x,y)) \nonumber\\ 
=   &~\PDec(\CleanLeft(\RightRaw(\MakePair(x,y)))) \nonumber \tag{Unfolding $\Right$} \\  
=&~\PDec(\CleanLeft(\ITE^{(\eps)}_0(\FirstBit(y),\PEnc(y),1\circ\PEnc(y)))).\label{equ: tech clean ite}
\end{align}
The last equation follows from the equation `equ: right raw`. 

To further simplify the equation `equ: tech clean ite`, we will perform a case study on ``dirty'' $\ITE$ using a strengthened form of the if-then-else case theorem. We need to prove that 
\begin{align}
& \PDec(\CleanLeft(\PEnc(y))) = y \\ 
& \PDec(\CleanLeft(1\circ \PEnc(y))) = y
\end{align}
By the equation `equ: tech clean penc` and the equation `equ: tech clean penc 1`, both of them are implied by $\PDec(\PEnc(y)) = y$, which is given by the correctness proposition for the pair-encoding $\Penc$. 

(\emph{Correctness of $\Left$}). We will prove that $\PV\vdash\Left(\MakePair(x,y))=x$. By the definition axiom of $\Left$, it suffices to show that $\PV$ proves:
\[
\TR(\TR(\ITR(\MakePair(x,y),\PEnc(\Right(\MakePair(x,y)))))) = x. 
\]
By the correctness of $\Right$, we know that $\Right(\MakePair(x,y)) = y$ and thus we need to prove in $\PV$ that: 
\[
\TR(\TR(\ITR(x\circ 11\circ \PEnc(y),\PEnc(y)))) = x.
\]
Note that by induction on $y$, it can be proved that: 
\begin{proposition}
$\PV\vdash \ITR(x\circ y,y) = x$. 
\end{proposition}
Thus, it suffices to prove in $\PV$ that $\TR(\TR(x\circ 11)) = x$, which can be proved by unfolding $\TR$'s.

The defining axioms are $x \circ \eps = x$, $x \circ s_i(y) = s_i(x \circ y)$, $\TR(\eps) = \eps$, $\TR(s_i(x)) = x$, $\ITR(x, \eps) = x$, $\ITR(x, s_i(y)) = \TR(\ITR(x, y))$, $x \# \eps = \eps$, $x \# s_i(y) = x \circ (x \# y)$ ($i \in \{0,1\}$). New functions are introduced by composition or by limited recursion on notation, the latter requiring an order-$(i-1)$ $\PV$ proof of $\ITR(h_i(\vec x, y, z), z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)) = \eps$. Equations are derived using (L0) reflexivity, (L1) symmetry, (L2) transitivity, (L3) congruence, (L4) substitution, the definition axioms, and the structural-induction rule: from $f_j(\vec x, \eps) = g(\vec x)$ and $f_j(\vec x, s_i(y)) = h_i(\vec x, y, f_j(\vec x, y))$ ($i \in \{0,1\}$, $j \in \{1,2\}$) infer $f_1(\vec x, y) = f_2(\vec x, y)$. The standard model is denoted $\M$; $t^\M$ is the interpretation of term $t$ in $\M$. $\FP$ is the class of polynomial-time computable functions. $\calF, \calF'$ are Cobham's class and its variant (with the modified bound $|h_i(\vec x, y, z)| \le |z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)|$).

Theorem (book label `thm: two var recursion`).

Let $g_{00}(\vec x),g_{01}(\vec x,y),g_{10}(\vec x,y)$ be $\PV$ functions, $h_{\alpha}(\vec x,y_1,y_2,z)$ and $k_\alpha(\vec x,y_1,y_2)$ for $\alpha\in\zo^2$ be $\PV$ functions. If 
\[
\PV\vdash \ITR(h_\alpha(\vec x,y_1,y_2,z),z\circ k_\alpha(\vec x,y_1,y_2)) = 0
\]
for every $\alpha\in\zo^2$, then there is a $\PV$ function $f(\vec x,y_1,y_2)$ such that the following equations are provable in $\PV$: 
\begin{compactitem}
\item $f(\vec x, \eps,\eps) = g_{00}(\vec x)$;
\item $f(\vec x, \eps, s_i(y)) = g_{01}(\vec x,s_i(y))$ for $i\in\zo$;
\item $f(\vec x, s_i(y),\eps) = g_{10}(\vec x,s_i(y))$ for $i\in\zo$; 
\item $f(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2)) = h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x, y_1,y_2,f(\vec x, y_1,y_2))$ for $i_1,i_2\in\zo$. 
\end{compactitem}
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We will define a function $f'(\vec x, y_1,y_2,w_1,w_2)$ as discussed above. That is, we will use the limited recursion rule on the auxiliary variable $w_2$ using the functions $g,h_0,h_1$, where $g(\vec x,y_1,y_2,w_1)$
    \begin{equation}
    =  \begin{cases}
        \eps & \Not(\Or(\IsEps(\ITR(y_1,w_1)),\IsEps(\ITR(y_2,w_1)))) \\ 
        g_{00}(\vec x) & \And(\IsEps(\ITR(y_1,w_1)),\IsEps(\ITR(y_2,w_1))) \\ 
        g_{01}(\vec x, \ITR(y_2,w_1)) & \And(\IsEps(\ITR(y_1,w_1)),\Not(\IsEps(\ITR(y_2,w_1)))) \\
        g_{10}(\vec x, \ITR(y_1,w_1))& \And(\Not(\IsEps(\ITR(y_1,w_1))),\IsEps(\ITR(y_2,w_1)))
    \end{cases}  
    \end{equation}
    and for $i\in\zo$, $h_i(\vec x, y_1, y_2, w_1, w_2, z)$
    \begin{equation}
    = \begin{cases}
        g(\vec x, \hat y_1,\hat y_2,\eps) &\Or(\IsEps(\hat y_1),\IsEps(\hat y_2))  \\
        h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x,\TR(\hat y_1),\TR(\hat y_2),z) & (\LastBit(\hat y_1),\LastBit(\hat y_2)) = (i_1,i_2)
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    where $\hat y_j \eqdef  \ITR(y_j,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2)))$ for $j\in\{1,2\}$. Note that the case study in defining $g$, $h_0$, and $h_1$ can be done by the if-then-else function. We will define the function $k_i(\vec x, y_1,y_2,w_1,w_2)$ as 
    \begin{equation}
    = \begin{cases}
        g(\vec x, \hat y_1,\hat y_2,\eps) & \Or(\IsEps(\hat y_1),\IsEps(\hat y_2)) \\
        k_{i_1i_2}(\vec x,\TR(\hat y_1),\TR(\hat y_2)) & (\LastBit(\hat y_1),\LastBit(\hat y_2)) = (i_1,i_2)
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation}

    \paragraph{Inequality for limited recursion.} We need to verify that $(g,h_0,h_1,k_0,k_1)$ satisfy that 
    \[
    \PV\vdash \ITR(h_i(\vec x, y_1,y_2,w_1,w_2,z),k_i(\vec x, y_1,y_2,w_1,w_2)) = 0
    \]
    for $i\in\zo$ to use the limited recursion rule. This is implied by the assumption, the fact that $\PV\vdash \ITR(x,x) = 0$, and the case study technique on $\ITE$ (see the theorem allowing case analysis via $\ITE$ and the remark generalising the if-then-else case analysis to multiple branches).

    \paragraph{Correctness.} As mentioned above, we will define 
    \[ f(\vec x,y_1,y_2) \eqdef f'(\vec x,y_1,y_2,y_1\circ y_2,y_1\circ y_2),
    \] 
    and it remains to verify that the equations in the theorem statement are provable in $\PV$. We sketch the proof of each equation: 
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item To see that $f(\vec x,\eps,\eps) = g_{00}(\vec x)$, notice that $f(\vec x,\eps,\eps)$ is equal to $g(\vec x, \eps,\eps,\eps)$. By the definition of $g$, we will obtain (after unfolding $\ITR,\IsEps$ and $\And$) that $g(\vec x,\eps,\eps,\eps) = g_{00}(\vec x)$. 
    \item To see that $f(\vec x, \eps, s_j(y)) = g_{01}(\vec x,s_j(y))$, notice that $f(\vec x,\eps,s_j(y))$ is equal to 
    \[
    f'(\vec x,\eps,s_j(y),\eps \circ s_j(y),\eps \circ s_j(y)) = f'(\vec x,\eps,s_j(y),s_j(y),s_j(y)).
    \]
    Since $\hat y_1=\ITR(\eps,s_j(y),s_j(y)) = \eps$, we know (by unfolding $\ITE$ in the definition of $h_j$) that this is $\PV$-provably equal to 
    \[
    g(\vec x,\eps, \ITR(s_j(y),\ITR(s_j(y),s_j(y))),\eps) = g(\vec x,\eps,s_j(y),\eps)
    \]
    (The equation follows from that $\ITR(x,x)=\eps$ and $\ITR(y,\eps) = y$ are provable in $\PV$.) By unfolding $g$ and $\ITE$'s (in the definition of $g$), we can prove in $\PV$ that $g(\vec x,\eps,s_j(y),\eps) = g_{01}(\vec x, s_j(y))$. 
    \item The case for $f(\vec x,s_j(y),\eps)=g_{10}(\vec x,s_j(y))$ is similar to the case above. 
    \item To see that $f(\vec x,s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2))=h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x,y_1,y_2,f(\vec x,y_1,y_2))$ for $i_1,i_2\in\zo$, notice that $\PV$ proves 
    \begin{align}
    &~ f(\vec x,s_{i_1}(y_1), s_{i_2}(y_2)) \\ 
    = &~f'(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ s_{i_2}(y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ s_{i_2}(y_2)) \\
    = &~f'(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2),s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2)) \\ 
    = &~h_{i_2}(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2),s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2,z) \label{equ: tech h j 2}
    \end{align}
    where 
    \begin{align}
    z & \eqdef f'(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2),s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2) \\
     & = f'(\vec x, y_1, y_2, y_1\circ y_2, y_1\circ y_2) \label{equ: tech z eq}\\ 
     & = f(\vec x, y_1,y_2).\label{equ: tech z f}
    \end{align}
    
    % (the equation `equ: tech z eq` can be proved in $\PV$ by unfolding the definition of $f$ and applying identities for $\ITR$, such as $\ITR(s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2) = \ITR(s_i(y_1\circ y_2), y_1\circ y_2)$ and $\ITR(s_{i_1}(y_1),\ITR(s_i(y_1\circ y_2), y_1\circ y_2)) = y_1$, $\ITR(x,x) = \eps$.)

    
    Here, the equation `equ: tech z eq` is non-trivial and will be deferred to the end of the proof. 
    
    Also, notice that  
    \begin{align}
    \hat y_1 &= \ITR(s_{i_1}(y_1),\ITR(s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2), s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2))) = s_{i_1}(y_1) \\ 
    \hat y_2 &= \ITR(s_{i_2}(y_2),\ITR(s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2), s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2))) = s_{i_2}(y_2)
    \end{align}
    By unfolding $h_{i_2}$ we can see that 
    \begin{equation}
        the equation `equ: tech h j 2` = h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x, y_1,y_2, z),
    \end{equation}
    which (together with the equation `equ: tech z f`) obtains the equation we need. 
    \end{compactitem}

    It remains to prove the equation `equ: tech z eq`. Indeed, we will prove a more general equation (which derives the equation `equ: tech z eq` by $z_1/y_1$ and $z_2/y_2$). 
    \begin{proposition}
    $\PV$ proves the following equation 
    \[ 
    f'(\vec x, s_{i_1}(z_1),s_{i_2}(z_2),s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2)
    = f'(\vec x, z_1, z_2, y_1\circ y_2, y_1\circ y_2).
    \] 
    \end{proposition}
    \begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
        Let $f_1(\vec x, z_1,z_2,y_1,y_2)$ and $f_2(\vec x, z_1,z_2,y_1,y_2)$ be the LHS and RHS of the equation, respectively. Notice that when $y_1$ and $y_2$ are substituted by $\eps$, the equation is provable in $\PV$ by simply unfolding $f'$. We then prove that 
        \begin{equation}
        f_1(\vec x,z_1,z_2,y_1,\eps) = f_2(\vec x,z_1,z_2,y_1,\eps).\label{equ: tech f1 f2 y1 eps}
        \end{equation}
        To see this, notice that both sides of the equation are identical to the function recursively defined on $y_1$ using some $\PV$ functions $g',h_0',h_1'$. Specifically, the base case is given by that $f_1(\vec x,z_1,z_2,\eps,\eps) = f_2(\vec x,z_1,z_2,\eps,\eps)$, and the induction step requires proving identities on $\ITR$, such as $\ITR(z,\ITR(s_{i_2}(s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2),s_{i_1}(y_1)\circ y_2)) = \TR(z)$.

        Subsequently, we prove
        \[
        f_1(\vec x,z_1,z_2,y_1,y_2) = f_2(\vec x,z_1,z_2,y_1,y_2)
        \]
        by showing that both sides of the equation are identical to the function recursively defined on $y_2$ using some $\PV$ functions $g'',h_0'',h_1''$. This time, the base case is given by the equation `equ: tech f1 f2 y1 eps`, while the induction case also requires proving identities on $\ITR$. 
    \end{proof}
    
    This completes the proof.
</informal_proof>

Theorem (book label `thm: ind multiple var`).

Let $f_1(\vec x,y_1,y_2),f_2(\vec x,y_1,y_2)$ be two $\PV$ functions. Let $g_{00}(\vec x)$, $g_{01}(\vec x,y)$, $g_{10}(\vec x,y)$, and $h_{\alpha}(\vec x,y_1,y_2,z)$, $\alpha\in\zo^2$ be $\PV$ functions. Suppose that for $j\in\{1,2\}$, $\PV$ proves that 
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $f_j(\vec x, \eps,\eps) = g_{00}(\vec x)$;
    \item $f_j(\vec x, \eps, s_j(y)) = g_{01}(\vec x,s_j(y))$ for $j\in\zo$;
    \item $f_j(\vec x, s_j(y),\eps) = g_{10}(\vec x,s_j(y))$ for $j\in\zo$; 
    \item $f_j(\vec x, s_{i_1}(y_1),s_{i_2}(y_2)) = h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x, y_1,y_2,f_j(\vec x, y_1,y_2))$ for $i_1,i_2\in\zo$.

    Then $\PV\vdash f_1(\vec x,y_1,y_2) = f_2(\vec x, y_1,y_2)$.

The proof idea of the multi-variable structural induction theorem closely follows the proof of Cook's two-variable recursion theorem. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, we define 
\begin{equation}
f_j'(\vec x,y_1,y_2,w_1,w_2) \eqdef f_j(\vec x,\ITR(y_1,\ITR(w_1,w_2)),\ITR(y_2,\ITR(w_1,w_2))).  
\end{equation}
We will prove that 
\begin{equation} 
\PV\vdash f'_0(\vec x,y_1,y_2,y_1\circ y_2,w_2) = f'_1(\vec x,y_1,y_2,y_1\circ y_2,w_2)\label{equ: tech aux equal ind}
\end{equation}
and thus the theorem follows by substituting $w_2$ with $y_1\circ y_2$.

\[
= \begin{cases}

& \quad \IsEps(\ITR(y_2,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2)))))=1 \\ 
    g_{01}(\vec x,\ITR(y_2,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2))))  & \IsEps(\ITR(y_1,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2)))) = 1\\ 
    g_{10}(\vec x,\ITR(y_1,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2)))) & \IsEps(\ITR(y_2,\ITR(w_1,s_i(w_2)))) = 1 \\ 
    h_{i_1i_2}(\vec x, \TR(\hat y_1),\TR(\hat y_2),z) & (\LastBit(\hat y_1),\LastBit(\hat y_2)) = (i_1,i_2)
\end{cases}
\]
where $w_1\eqdef y_1\circ y_2$, $\hat y_j \eqdef \ITR(y_j,w_1,s_i(w_2))$ for $j\in\{1,2\}$. It can be verified (similar to the proof of the multi-variable structural induction theorem) that both LHS and RHS of the equation `equ: tech aux equal ind` are identical to the function recursively defined by $g'(\vec x,y_1,y_2),h_0(\vec x,y_1,y_2,w_2,z),h_1(\vec x,y_1,y_2,w_2,z)$ inductively on the variable $w_2$.
</informal_proof>

\[ 
e\equiv ``\EQ(x, y) \Ra s_i(z)\Ra x=y".

    \begin{align*}
    &~[x = y,  y = z\vdash x = z]_\PV \\
    \equiv&~``\EQ(y,z)\Ra \EQ(x,y)\Ra \EQ(x,z)=1" \\ 
    \equiv&~``\EQ(y,z)\Ra \ITE(\EQ(x,y),1,\EQ(x,z))=\EQ(x,z)" \\ 
    \equiv&~``\ITE(\EQ(y,z), \EQ(x,z), \ITE(\EQ(x,y),1,\EQ(x,z))) = \ITE(\EQ(x,y),1,\EQ(x,z))".
    \end{align*}

    \begin{align*}
    & f(\eps,y,z) \eqdef \ITE(\EQ(\eps,y), 1, \EQ(\eps,z)),\quad f(x,\eps,z)\eqdef \ITE(\EQ(x,\eps),1,\EQ(x,z)),\\ 
    & \quad f(x,y,\eps) \eqdef \ITE(\EQ(x,y),1,\EQ(x,\eps)) \\ 
    & f(s_i(x),s_j(y),s_k(z)) \eqdef \begin{cases}

Again, it suffices to prove that $\PV\vdash[x=y\vdash t[z/x]=t[z/y]]_\PV$, or equivalently: 
    \[

    \]
    Indeed, we will prove a stronger result (by the correctness of $\EQ$ under conditional-equation form) that 
    \[
    \PV\vdash \EQ(x,y)\Ra t[z/x] = t[z/y].
    \]
    Suppose that $z,\vec w$ are the variables that occurred in $t$, and $f_t(z,\vec w) = t$ is the function defined from $t$ using the composition rule in $\PV$. It suffices to prove that
    \[
    \PV\vdash \EQ(x,y)\Ra f_t(x,\vec w) = f_t(y,\vec w),
    \]
    or equivalently $\PV\vdash \ITE(\EQ(x,y), f_t(y,\vec w),f_t(x,\vec w)) = f_t(x,\vec w)$.

\[
\EQL(\eps,s_i(y)) = \EQL(s_j(x),\eps) = 0,\quad \EQL(s_i(x),s_j(y)) = \EQL(x,y). 
\]

    \begin{align*}
    & \Suf(x,\eps) \eqdef \eps,\quad \Suf(\eps,y) \eqdef \eps \\ 
    & \Suf(s_i(x),s_j(y)) \eqdef s_i(\Suf(x,y)). 
    \end{align*}
    It can be proved by induction on $x$ that $\Suf(x,y\circ x)=x$. Moreover, we can prove the following properties of $\Suf$:

    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $\EQL(y,z)\Ra \Suf(x,y) = \Suf(x,z)$. 
    \item $\Suf(x, y\circ x) = x$.
    \item $\Suf(x, s_i(y)) = \LastBit(\ITR(x,y))\circ \Suf(x,y)$, $i\in\zo$.

    \begin{align*}
    & g(\eps,x,y,\vec w) = f_t(x,\vec w), \\
    & g(s_i(z),x,y,\vec w) = \begin{cases}
        f_t(x,\vec w) & \EQ(\LastBit(\ITR(x,z)),\LastBit(\ITR(y,z))) = 1;\\
        g(z,x,y,\vec w) & \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    The RHS of the equation `equ: tech generalized eq sub` is identical to $g$.

Notice that by a technical proposition collecting useful properties of conditional equations: 
    \begin{align}
       &~\EQ(\Suf(x,s_i(z)),\Suf(y,s_i(z)))\nonumber \\ 
    =  &~\EQ(\LastBit(\ITR(x,z))\circ \Suf(x,z),\LastBit(\ITR(y,z))\circ \Suf(y,z)). \label{equ: tech eq first bit}
    \end{align}

    \begin{align*}
    the equation `equ: tech eq first bit` &= \And(\EQ(\LastBit(\ITR(x,z)),\LastBit(\ITR(y,z))),\EQ(\Suf(x,z),\Suf(y,z))).
    \end{align*}

    \begin{align*}

    =   &~\ITR(x,s_i(z))\circ(\LastBit(\ITR(y,z))\circ\Suf(y,z)) \tag{a technical proposition collecting useful properties of conditional equations}. \\ 
    =   &~\ITR(x,s_i(z))\circ\LastBit(\ITR(y,z))\circ\Suf(y,z)
    \end{align*}

    \begin{align*}
    & \begin{cases}
      f_t(\TR(z')\circ \LastBit(z'')\circ\Suf(y,z),\vec w)  & \substack{\displaystyle\And(\EQ(\LastBit(z'),\LastBit(z'')),\\ 
      \displaystyle\EQ(\Suf(x,z),\Suf(y,z)))=1} \\ 
      f_t(x,\vec w) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases} \\ 
    & = \begin{cases}

        f_t(x,\vec w) & \text{otherwise}; 
    \end{cases} \\ 
    & \equiv \begin{cases}
        \LHS[the equation `equ: tech generalized eq sub`] & \EQ(\LastBit(z'),\LastBit(z''))=1; \\ 
        f_t(x,\vec w) & \text{otherwise}; 
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    
    To see that this suffices, we can substitute 
    \[ 
    z'/\ITR(x,z),\quad z''/\ITR(y,z)
    \] 
    so that according to the properties we proved above, the equation shows exactly that the LHS of the equation `equ: tech generalized eq sub` is identical to the function $g$ recursively defined as above. 

    Finally, we prove the equation above by a case study on $z'$ and $z''$ using the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable). In all cases that $\LastBit(z')\ne \LastBit(z'')$, both sides of the consequence of the conditional equation evaluates to $f_t(x,\vec w)$. Now we consider the cases that $\LastBit(z')=\LastBit(z'')$, for instance, with the substitution $z'/s_0(z')$ and $z''/s_0(z'')$. In such case, the LHS of the equation evaluates to  
    \[
    \begin{cases}
      f_t(z'\circ 0 \circ\Suf(y,z),\vec w)  & \EQ(\Suf(x,z),\Suf(y,z)))=1; \\ 
      f_t(x,\vec w) & \text{otherwise},
    \end{cases}
    \]
    while the RHS evaluates to 
    \begin{align*}
    &~\ITE(\EQ(\Suf(x,z),\Suf(y,z)),f_t(s_0(z')\circ \Suf(y,z),\vec w),f_t(x,\vec w)) \\
    =&~\begin{cases}
      f_t(s_0(z')\circ\Suf(y,z),\vec w)  & \EQ(\Suf(x,z),\Suf(y,z)))=1; \\ 
      f_t(x,\vec w) & \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    Since $z'\circ 0=s_0(z')$, we can prove that they are identical by a case study on $\ITE$ using the theorem allowing case analysis via $\ITE$. This completes the proof.
</informal_proof>

Lemma.

The elimination rule $(\perp_e)$ of $\perp$ is admissible. That is, for any $\Gamma$ and any formula $\alpha$, suppose that $\PV\vdash[\Gamma,\lnot\alpha\vdash \bot]_\PV$, then $\PV\vdash[\Gamma\vdash\alpha]_\PV$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We will prove that the axiom of double negation elimination is admissible in $\PV$, that is: 
    \[
    \PV\vdash[\Gamma\vdash \lnot\lnot\alpha\to\alpha]_\PV. 
    \]
    To see that this suffices, notice that the elimination rule $(\perp_e)$ can be simulated by the following proof tree using double negation elimination using the introduction and elimination rules of $\to$ that have already proved to be admissible: 
    \begin{prooftree}
    \AxiomC{}
    \UnaryInfC{$\Gamma\vdash\lnot\lnot\alpha\to\alpha$}
    \AxiomC{$\Gamma,\lnot\alpha\vdash\perp$}
    \RightLabel{($\to_i$)}
    \UnaryInfC{$\Gamma\vdash\lnot\lnot\alpha$}
    \RightLabel{($\to_e$)}
    \BinaryInfC{$\Gamma\vdash\alpha$}
    \end{prooftree}
    Moreover, by the admissibility of weakening (W), it suffices to prove the admissibility of the case $\Gamma=\varnothing$. That is, 
    \begin{align*}
        & \PV\vdash [\vdash\lnot\lnot\alpha\to\alpha]_\PV \\
    \iff & \PV\vdash \ITE(\ITE(\ITE([\alpha]_\PV,0,1),0,1),[\alpha]_\PV,1) = 1. 
    \end{align*}
    Furthermore, it suffices to prove the more general version: 
    \begin{align*}
        & \PV\vdash \IsNotEps(x)\Ra \ITE(\ITE(\ITE(x,0,1),0,1),x,1) = 1,
    \end{align*}
    which can be proved by a case study on $x$ using the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable).
</informal_proof>

The conditional equation $a \Rightarrow b = c$ is encoded as $\ITE(a, c, b) = b$ where $\ITE$ is the $\PV$ if-then-else function (returning $b$ on $a = 1$ and $c$ on $a = 0$ at its rightmost bit). The aim of this chapter is to show that all standard structural and equational rules of predicate logic are admissible under this translation. $\IsEps$ and $\IsNotEps$ are the $\PV$ predicates testing whether a string equals $\eps$. Background on $\PV$ is summarized in the glossary.

Lemma.

The structural induction rule $(\Ind_2)$ is admissible. That is, for any terms $t_1,t_2$, $\Gamma$, and variables $x_1,x_2$, suppose that $\PV$ proves 
\begin{compactitem}
\item $[\Gamma\vdash t_1[x_j/\eps]=t_2[x_j/\eps]]_\PV$, where $j\in\{1,2\}$. 
\item $[\Gamma, t_1=t_2\vdash t_1[x_1/s_{i_1}(x_1),x_2/s_{i_2}(x_2)]=t_2[x_1/s_{i_1}(x_1),x_2/s_{i_2}(x_2)]]_\PV$, where $i_1,i_2\in\zo$. 
\end{compactitem}
Then $\PV\vdash [\Gamma\vdash t_1=t_2]_\PV$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
By the admissibility of the permutation rule, we can change the second bullet to $[t_1=t_2,\Gamma\vdash t_1[x_1/s_{i_1}(x_1),x_2/s_{i_2}(x_2)]=t_2[x_1/s_{i_1}(x_1),x_2/s_{i_2}(x_2)]]_\PV$. Moreover, we can (without loss of generality) replace $t_1,t_2$ by the $\PV$ functions symbols $f_1,f_2$ defined by $f_i(x_1,x_2,\vec w)=t_i$, $i\in\{1,2\}$, where $\vec w$ denote other variables in $t_1,t_2$. For simplicity, we will ignore $\vec w$ in the proof and write $f_i(x_1,x_2)$. 
    
    Let $\Gamma=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)$. We will prove the admissibility in $\PV$ by induction on $n$ (in the meta-theory). Concretely, we will prove that for any $\PV$ terms $u_1,\dots,u_n$, if $\PV$ proves 
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $\IsNotEps(u_i) = 1$ for any $i\in[n]$, 
    \item $u_n\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(\eps,x_2),f_2(\eps,x_2))=1$, 
    \item $u_n\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,\eps),f_2(x_1,\eps))=1$,
    \item $u_n\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2))\Ra \EQ(f_1(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)),f_2(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)))=1$, for any $i_1,i_2\in\zo$, 
    \end{compactitem}
    Then $\PV$ proves $u_n\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)) = 1$. (Note that by instantiating $u_i\eqdef [\beta_i]_\PV$ for $i\in[n]$ we can derive the lemma.) 
    
    \paragraph{Base case.} We first consider the case $n=1$. The case for $\Gamma=\varnothing$ can be derived from this case, which is left as an exercise. Note that we need to prove that if $\PV$ proves for any $\PV$ term $u$, 
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $\IsNotEps(u) = 1$, 
    \item $u\Ra \EQ(f_1(\eps,x_2),f_2(\eps,x_2))=1$, 
    \item $u\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,\eps),f_2(x_1,\eps))=1$,
    \item $u\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2))\Ra \EQ(f_1(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)),f_2(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)))=1$, for any $i_1,i_2\in\zo$, 
    \end{compactitem}
    then $\PV\vdash u\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2))=1$. That is: 
    \begin{equation}
        \ITE(u, 1, \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2))) = \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)).
    \end{equation}
    We will prove the alternative equation: 
    \begin{equation}
        \ITE(u, \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)), 1) = 1
    \end{equation}
    in $\PV$, and it is left as an exercise to prove that this suffices. 
    
    We will prove the equation by simultaneous induction on $x_1$ and $x_2$ using the multi-variable structural induction theorem. Let $g_{00} = g_{01}(x) = g_{10}(y) = 1$, and $h_{i_1i_2}(x,y,z) = \ITE(z, 1, 0)$ for $i_1,i_2\in\zo$. It is easy to see that the RHS of ($\star$) is identical to the function defined recursively from $g_{j_1j_2}$ and $h_{i_1i_2}$. Moreover, we can easily see that $\PV$ proves:  
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $\ITE(u,\EQ(f_1(\eps,\eps),f_2(\eps,\eps)),1) = g_{00} = 1$,
    \item $\ITE(u,\EQ(f_1(\eps,s_j(x_2)),f_2(\eps,s_j(x_2))),1) = g_{01}(s_j(x_2)) = 1$,
    \item $\ITE(u,\EQ(f_1(s_j(x_1),\eps),f_2(s_j(x_1),\eps)),1) = g_{01}(s_j(x_1)) = 1$,
    \end{compactitem}
    from the assumption. Therefore, it suffices to prove that 
    \begin{align}
      &~\ITE(u,\EQ(f_1(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)), f_2(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2))),1) \nonumber \\
    = &~\ITE(\ITE(u,\EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)),1), 1, 0). \label{equ: tech ind recursion} 
    \end{align}

    We will first prove a more general result: 
    \begin{proposition}\label{prop: tech ind rec general}
    $\PV\vdash (x\Ra y\Ra z = 1) \Ra \ITE(x,z,1) = \ITE(\ITE(x,y,1),1,0)$. 
    \end{proposition}
    This can be proved by a simple case study on $x$, $y$, and $z$ using the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable). 

    Finally, with the substitution 
    \begin{align*} 
    & x/u \\ 
    & y/\EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)) \\ 
    & z/\EQ(f_1(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)),f_2(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)))
    \end{align*}
    we can see that the antecedent of a generalized recursion-based induction proposition is exactly the second bullet of the assumption, and the consequence is exactly the equation `equ: tech ind recursion` that we need to prove. This concludes the base case by Modus Ponens (see the Modus Ponens proposition for $\PV$ conditional equations). 
    
    \paragraph{Induction case.} Our strategy is to ``merge'' $u_{n+1}$ and $u_n$ in the antecedents of the conditional equation so that it reduces to the case for $|\Gamma|=n$. Concretely, we will prove the following meta-theorem of $\PV$:
    
    \begin{proposition}\label{prop: tech and merge}
    Let $t_1,t_2,t_c,t_c'$ be terms such that $\PV\vdash\IsNotEps(t_c) = 1$ and $\PV\vdash\IsNotEps(t_c') = 1$. Then $\PV\vdash t_c\Ra t_c'\Ra t_1=t_2$ if and only if $\PV\vdash \And(t_c,t_c')\Ra t_1=t_2$.     
    \end{proposition}

    To see that this suffices, notice that by applying the meta-theorem on both the premise and the conclusion of the rule, it suffices to derive from   
    \begin{align*}
    & \PV\vdash \IsNotEps(u_i)=1 \quad (i\in[n-1]) \\
    & \PV\vdash \IsNotEps(\And(u_{n+1}, u_n)) = 1 \\  
    & \PV\vdash \And(u_{n+1},u_n)\Ra u_{n-1}\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(\eps,x_2),f_2(\eps,x_2))=1 \\ 
    & \PV\vdash \And(u_{n+1},u_n)\Ra u_{n-1}\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,\eps),f_2(x_1,\eps))=1 \\ 
    & \PV\vdash \And(u_{n+1},u_n)\Ra u_{n-1}\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2))\Ra \\ 
    & \quad \quad \EQ(f_1(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)),f_2(s_{i_1}(x_1),s_{i_2}(x_2)))=1 \quad(i_1,i_2\in\zo)
    \end{align*}
    that $\PV\vdash \And(u_{n+1},u_{n})\Ra u_{n-1}\Ra \dots\Ra u_1\Ra \EQ(f_1(x_1,x_2),f_2(x_1,x_2)) = 1$, which is true by the induction hypothesis and the fact that if $\PV\vdash \IsNotEps(u) = 1$ and $\PV\vdash \IsNotEps(u') = 1$, then $\PV\vdash \IsNotEps(\And(u,u'))=1$. 

    It remains to prove a technical proposition for merging conjunction-like conditional equations. We will only prove the $(\Rightarrow)$ directly, and the converse can be proved using the same approach. Consider the following more general version: 
    \begin{proposition}
    $\PV\vdash \IsNotEps(z_1)\Ra\IsNotEps(z_2)\Ra (z_1\Ra z_2\Ra x = y)\Ra \And(z_1,z_2)\Ra x= y$. 
    \end{proposition}
    This can be proved by a case study on $z_1$ and $z_2$ using the theorem of proof by case study (every equation provable when each top-bit case is provable). <informal_proof>
We prove by induction on the depth of the substitution formula $\varphi$. 
    
    \subparagraph{Base case.} Suppose that $\varphi$ is atomic, i.e., it is either $\bot$ or a $\PV$ equation $u=v$. Note that the case for $\varphi\equiv \bot$ is trivial by the assumption rule (A). Consider the case for $\varphi\equiv ``u = v"$ and $\varphi' \equiv ``u' = v'"$, and it suffices to prove the admissibility of $(\hat =_/)$ as $(\hat =_/^{-1})$ can be simulated by $(\hat =_/)$ with substitution formula of the same depth. Let $z$ be a fresh variable and $\hat u$ and $\hat v$ be the terms satisfying that 
    \[
    \hat u[z/y] = u', \hat u[z/x] = u, \; \hat v[z/y] = v', \hat v[z/x] = v.
    \]
    Notice that we can prove $\Gamma,x=y, u =v \vdash u = u'$ by the proof tree (where all structural rules are omitted):
    \begin{prooftree}
    \AxiomC{}
    \RightLabel{($=_/$)}
    \UnaryInfC{$\Gamma,x=y,u=v\vdash \hat u[z/x] = \hat u[z/y]$}
    \end{prooftree}
    Similarly, we can prove that $\Gamma,x=y,u=v\vdash v=v'$. Therefore by the cut rule and the symmetricity and transitivity of equality, we can prove $\Gamma,x=y,u=v\vdash u'=v'$. 

    \subparagraph{Induction case.} Suppose that $\varphi$ is of form $\beta\to\alpha$ and $\varphi'\equiv \beta'\to\alpha'$. By the induction hypothesis, we know that both $(\hat =_/)$ and $(\hat =_/^{-1})$ are admissible if the substitution formula is $\alpha$, $\alpha'$, $\beta$ or $\beta'$. It suffices to prove the admissibility of $(\hat =_s)$ with $\varphi$ being the substitution formula, i.e., 
    \[
    \Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha\vdash\beta'\to\alpha'. 
    \]

    By the introduction rule of implication, it suffices to prove that $\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta'\vdash\alpha'$. We then apply the cut rule with $\beta$ being the cut formula, so that it generates two subgoals to resolve: 
    \begin{itemize}
    \item[(\emph{Subgoal} 1):] $\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta'\vdash\beta$. This is provable by the induction hypothesis, as we can apply $(\hat =_/^{-1})$ with $\beta'$ being the substitution formula. 
    \item[(\emph{Subgoal} 2):] $\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta\vdash\alpha'$. We apply the cut rule again with $\alpha$ being the cut formula, so that it further generates two subgoals:  
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(\emph{Subgoal 2.1}):] $\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta\vdash\alpha$. Notice that this can be proved by Modus Ponens on two assumptions, which can be implemented by the elimination rule of $\to$: 
        \begin{prooftree}
        \AxiomC{}
        \RightLabel{(A)}
        \UnaryInfC{$\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta\vdash\beta\to\alpha$}
        \AxiomC{}
        \RightLabel{(A)}
        \UnaryInfC{$\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta\vdash\beta$}
        \RightLabel{($\to_e$)}
        \BinaryInfC{$\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta\vdash\alpha$}
        \end{prooftree}
        \item[(\emph{Subgoal 2.2}):] $\Gamma,x=y,\beta\to\alpha,\beta',\beta,\alpha\vdash\alpha'$. This is provable by the induction hypothesis, as we can apply $(\hat =_/)$ with $\alpha$ being the substitution formula. 
    \end{itemize}
    \end{itemize}
    This completes all subgoals and leads to the lemma.

Both $(\CPV)$ and $(\CPVi)$ are admissible in $\PVPL$.

\[
\Gamma,\beta\to\alpha, [\beta]_\PV=1\vdash \alpha. 
\]
Using the cut rule it suffices to prove that $\Gamma,\beta\to\alpha,\alpha, [\beta]_\PV=1\vdash [\alpha]_\PV$, which again follows from the induction hypothesis.

Lemma (book label `lmm: bounding lists`).

$\PV\vdash \ITR(\ell :: x, \ell \circ (11\circ \PEnc(x))) = \eps.$
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
By unfolding the definition of $\Append$ (i.e.~$\ell :: x$), subsequently unfolding $\MakePair$, and applying the associativity of concatenation (the lemma $\PV \vdash (x \circ y) \circ z = x \circ (y \circ z)$ (associativity of concatenation)), it suffices to prove that 
\begin{equation}
\PV\vdash \ITR(\ell\circ 11\circ \PEnc(x),\ell\circ 11\circ \PEnc(x)) = \eps. 
\end{equation}
This follows from $\PV\vdash\ITR(x,x) = \eps$ using (L4) substitution, and $\ITR(x,x)=\eps$ can be proved in $\PV$ using the lemma $\PV \vdash \ITR(x, z \circ x) = \eps$ and the lemma $\PV \vdash \eps \circ x = x$ ($\eps$ is a left identity for concatenation).
</informal_proof>

Lemma.

The assignment axiom scheme is admissible in $\PVPL$: 
\[
\frac{}{\Omega, \varphi[x_i/\Suf(e,\omega)]\vdash \varphi^{[\bmlet{x_i}{e}]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k))}}
\]

\begin{align*}
    & [\bmlet{x_i}{e}]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k)) \\ 
=   ~& \MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1},\Suf(e,\omega),x_{i+1},\dots,x_k).
\end{align*}
Moreover, notice that $\PV$ also proves
\[
\varphi^{\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1},\Suf([e],\omega),x_{i+1},\dots,x_k)} = \varphi[x_i/\Suf(e,\omega)]. 
\]

This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Lemma.

Let $c$ be an $\IMP(\PV)$ program, $P$ be the program $\bmfor{x_i}{e}{c}$. The rule of for-loop, formalized as follows, is admissible in $\PVPL$:
\[
\frac{\Omega, \varphi[x_i/s_j(x_i)]\vdash \varphi^{[c]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k))}\quad (\forall j\in\zo)}{\Omega, \varphi[x_i/\Suf(e,\omega)]\vdash \varphi[x_i/\eps]^{[P]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k))}}
\]
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
Let $f_\mathsf{iter}$, $f_{\mathsf{loop}}$, and $f$ be the functions in the translation of for-loop (see the section on compiling $\IMP(\PV)$ programs to $\PV$ functions) for $P$; in particular, $f(\omega,\pi) = [P]_\PV(\omega,\pi)$ and it satisfies that 
    \[
    f(\omega,\pi) = f_\mathsf{loop}(\omega,\MakeTuple(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_{i-1},[e]_\PV^\pi,\pi_{i+1},\dots,\pi_k),[e]_\PV^\pi),
    \]
    where $f_\mathsf{loop}$ is recursively defined and satisfies that 
    \begin{align*}
    f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,\eps) &= \pi \\ 
    f_{\sf loop}(\omega, \pi, s_i(y)) &= \MakeTuple(\Suf(f_\mathsf{iter}(\omega,z)_1,\omega), \dots, \Suf(f_\mathsf{iter}(\omega,z)_k,\omega)) \\
    & \quad \quad (z\eqdef f_\mathsf{loop}(\omega,\pi,y)) \\     f_{\sf iter}(\omega,\pi) &= \MakeTuple(\pi'_1,\dots,\pi'_{i-1},\TR(\pi'_i),\pi'_{i+1},\dots,\pi'_k) \\ 
    & \quad \quad (\pi'\eqdef [c]_\PV(\omega,\pi))
    \end{align*}
    
    We first prove, by induction on $y$, that after $|y|$ iteration of the for-loop, $x_i$ will be $\ITR(x_i,y)$, $x_j=\Suf(x_j,\omega)$, and the invariant $\varphi$ still holds. Formally, let $\pi\eqdef \MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k)$: 
    \begin{align}
    & \Omega,\varphi\vdash \ITR(y,x_i) = \eps \to (f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y))_i = \ITR(x_i,y);\label{equ: for loop index} \\ 
    & \Omega,\varphi\vdash \ITR(y,x_i) = \eps \to (f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y))_j = \ITR((f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y))_j,\omega);\label{equ: for loop length} \\
    & \Omega,\varphi\vdash \ITR(y,x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y)}.\label{equ: for loop invariant} 
    \end{align}
    for $j\in[k]$. 
    
    Note that the equation `equ: for loop index` formalizes that $x_i$ will be $\ITR(x_i,y)$ after $|y|$ iterations; the base case is straightforward, while the induction case requires that $([c]_\PV(\omega,\pi))_i = \pi_i$, which is true as $x_i$ is not changed in the for-loop by the \emph{read-only restriction}, and can be formally proved by structural induction on the definition of $c$ (in the meta-theory). Similarly, the equation `equ: for loop length` formalizes that all variables are bounded by $\omega$, which can be proved by induction on $y$ and apply the proposition that $\IMP(\PV)$ programs are bounded. 
    
    the equation `equ: for loop invariant` formalizes that the loop invariant $\varphi$ holds throughout the loop; the base case is also straightforward, so we will only explain the proof of the induction case of the equation `equ: for loop invariant`. That is, suppose that 
    \begin{equation} 
    \Omega,\varphi,\ITR(y,x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y)},\label{equ: tech for loop assumptions}
    \end{equation} 
    we need to prove for $\sigma\in\zo$ that
    \[
    \ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,s_\sigma(y))},
    \]
    which is equivalent to say (by the definition axiom of $f_{\sf loop}$) that: 
    \[
    \ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{\MakeTuple(\Suf(f_\mathsf{iter}(\omega,z)_1,\omega), \dots, \Suf(f_\mathsf{iter}(\omega,z)_k,\omega))}
    \]
    where $z\eqdef f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y)$. By the equation `equ: for loop length` and the proposition that $\IMP(\PV)$ programs are bounded, we know that all coordinates of $f_{\sf iter}(\omega,z)$ are bounded by $\omega$, and thus it suffices to prove that $\ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{f_\mathsf{iter}(\omega,z)}$, i.e., for $\pi'\eqdef[c]_\PV(\omega,z)$:
    \begin{equation}
    \ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps \to \varphi^{\MakeTuple(\pi'_1,\dots,\pi'_{i-1},\TR(\pi'_i),\pi'_{i+1},\dots,\pi'_n)}.\label{equ: tech for loop goal} 
    \end{equation}

    Suppose that $\ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps$, we also know that $\ITR(y,x_i) = \eps$. Recall that we have $\pi'_i = z_i = f_{\sf loop}(\omega,\pi,y)$ as the variable $x_i$ is read-only in the program $c$. By the equation `equ: for loop index` and $\ITR(y,x_i) = \eps$, we further know that $\pi'_i = \ITR(x_i,y)$. Moreover, we know by $\ITR(s_\sigma(y),x_i) = \eps$ that $\pi'_i\ne \eps$, and thus $\pi'_i = s_{\sigma'}(\TR(\pi'_i))$ for some $\sigma'\in\zo$. This allows us to apply the premise 
    \[
    \Omega, \varphi[x_i/s_{\sigma'}(x_i)]\vdash \varphi^{[c]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k))}
    \]
    by substituting $x_i/\TR(\pi'_i)$ and $x_j/z_j$ for any $j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}$. 

    Let $\delta$ be the aforementioned substitution, we can see that $\Omega[\delta]$ is provable by the equation `equ: for loop length`, $\varphi[x_i/s_{\sigma'}(x_i)][\delta]$ is given by the antecedent the equation `equ: tech for loop assumptions` of the assertion we are proving, and $\varphi^{[c]_\PV(\omega,\MakeTuple(x_1,\dots,x_k))}[\delta]$ is exactly what we need to prove (see the equation `equ: tech for loop goal`). This completes the induction case.
</informal_proof>

Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Theorem.

The following rules are admissible in $\PVPL$. Suppose that $\Gamma=\Gamma',\IsList(\ell) = 1$, then:  
\begin{align}
& (\exists_i):\quad \frac{\Gamma\vdash \varphi[y/t]\quad \Gamma\vdash [t\in\ell]}{\Gamma\vdash \exists y\in\ell:\varphi}\\  & (\exists_e):\quad\frac{\Gamma\vdash\exists y\in\ell:\varphi\quad \Gamma,[z\in\ell], \varphi[y/z]\vdash\psi}{\Gamma\vdash \psi} 
\end{align}
where in $(\exists_i)$ $t$ is an arbitrary term, and in $(\exists_e)$ $z$ must be a fresh variable that has no occurrence in $\Gamma,\varphi,\psi,y$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We first consider the introduction rule $(\exists_i)$. Indeed, we will show that the assertion 
\[
\IsList(\ell'),\varphi[y/t]\vdash [t\in\ell']\to \exists y\in\ell':\varphi
\]
is provable in $\PVPL$, where $t'$ is a fresh variable that has no occurrence in $\varphi,t$. The admissibility of $(\exists_i)$ follows from the provability of the assertion. 

We will prove the assertion by induction on $\ell'$ using the corollary giving structural induction on lists in $\PVPL$. In the base case, i.e., $\ell'/\varnothing$, it is easy to see by the definition of the membership relation (and subsequently the definition axioms of $\Find_x$) that $[t\in\varnothing]$ is false. In the induction case, suppose that we have $\IsList(\ell'),\varphi[y/t]$ and $[t\in\ell']\to\exists y\in\ell':\varphi$ in the antecedent, we need to prove that 
\[
[t\in\ell' :: u]\to\exists y\in\ell' :: u:\varphi. 
\]
We introduce $[t\in\ell' :: u]$ as an assumption and aim to prove $\exists y\in\ell' :: u:\varphi$. We perform a case study on whether $t=u$ (recall that excluded middle is available by the cut rule and proof by contradiction, see the remark on excluded middle in feasible mathematics). 
\begin{compactitem} 
\item If $t=u$, we can see $\varphi[y/u]$ (by rewriting), and thus $\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell' :: u) = s_0(u)\ne \eps$, which means that $\exists y\in\ell' :: u:\varphi$ by the definition as well as the comprehension of $\PV$ translation in $\PVPL$ (see the comprehension lemma for $\PVPL$). 
\item If $t\ne u$, we can see that $\Find_t(\ell' :: u) = \Find_t(\ell')$, so that $[t\in \ell' :: u]$ implies that $[t\in\ell']$. By the induction hypothesis (and the elimination rule of implication), we can show that $\exists y\in\ell':\varphi$. This implies the goal $\exists y\in\ell' :: u:\varphi$ by a case study on whether $\varphi[y/u]$ holds. 
\end{compactitem}

Next, we prove that the elimination rule $(\exists_e)$ is admissible. From the premise that $\Gamma\vdash\exists y\in\ell :\varphi$ and the definition of the existential quantifier, we know that $\Gamma\vdash \Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell)\ne\varnothing$, which, by the correctness of $\Find_f$, deduces that 
\[ 
\Gamma\vdash[\varphi]_\PV(y/\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))) = 1.
\]
By the comprehension rule of the $\PV$ translation, we further know that 
\[
\Gamma\vdash \varphi[y/\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))]. 
\]
Similarly, we have that $\Gamma\vdash [\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))\in \ell]$.

By the substitution $z/\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))$ to the second premise, we can prove the assertion
\[
\Gamma,[\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))\in\ell],\varphi[y/\TR(\Find_{[\varphi]_\PV}(\ell))]\vdash\psi. 
\]
Notice that all formulas in the antecedent are provable from $\Gamma$ as we demonstrated above. Therefore, by the cut rule, we can conclude that $\Gamma\vdash\psi$.
</informal_proof>

Proposition (book label `prop: tech itrl s`).

$\PV\vdash \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y)) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
This can be proved by induction on $y$. The equation trivially holds when $y=\eps$ by unfolding the LHS. Suppose that the equation holds for $y$, notice that 
    \[
    \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(s_0(y))) = \Tail(\ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y))) 
    \]
    and 
    \[
    \ITRL(\ell, s_0(y)) = \Tail(\ITRL(\ell, y)). 
    \]
    Since $\ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y)) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$ by the assumption hypothesis, we can prove the induction case by applying the $\PVPL$ axioms of equality.
</informal_proof>

Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Proposition (book label `prop: tech itrl s`).

$\PV\vdash \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y)) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$.
informal_proof:
This can be proved by induction on $y$. The equation trivially holds when $y=\eps$ by unfolding the LHS. Suppose that the equation holds for $y$, notice that 
    \[
    \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(s_0(y))) = \Tail(\ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y))) 
    \]
    and 
    \[
    \ITRL(\ell, s_0(y)) = \Tail(\ITRL(\ell, y)). 
    \]
    Since $\ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(y)) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$ by the assumption hypothesis, we can prove the induction case by applying the $\PVPL$ axioms of equality.

    f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ell :: u) = h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR(\ell :: u))), 
    \]
    where the LHS is exactly $f(\vec x,\ell :: u)$ by the definition axiom of $f$.
</informal_proof>

<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Lemma (\emph{Subgoal} 1).

$\PV\vdash f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))) = f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ell))$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
Since $\PV\vdash \ITR(\ell,\ell)=\eps$, the RHS of the equation is $\PV$-provably equal to $f'(\vec x,\ell,\eps)$, and by the definition axiom of $f'$ it is further $\PV$-provably equal to $g(\vec x)$.  

    As for the LHS, notice that $\PV\vdash \IsEps(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))) = 0$ by unfolding $\ell :: u$ and proving basic properties about $\ITR$. By a technical proposition unfolding the conditional non-$\eps$ form, we know that  
    \begin{align*}
    & f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))) \\ 
    = &\begin{cases}
        g(\vec x) & \Or(\IsEps(\hat\ell), \IsEps(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))))  \\ 
        h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR( \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell)))) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    where $\hat\ell\eqdef \ITRL(\ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, \TR(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell)))))$. Note that  
    \[
    \EQL(\ITR(\ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))), s_0(\ell)) = 1, 
    \]
    and the proof is left as an exercise.\marginnote{Hint: \textcolor{hint}{Using a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$.}} By $\EQL(x,y) = 1\Ra \ITRL(\ell, x) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$ we can further prove that 
    \[
    \hat\ell = \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell)),
    \]
    which is further equal to $\ITRL(\ell, \ell)=\eps$. Therefore by unfolding the equation from a technical proposition unfolding the conditional non-$\eps$ form we have $f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))) = g(\vec x)$.
</informal_proof>

<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Lemma (book label `lmm: tech ind list eps case`).

$\PVPL$ proves $\Gamma,\IsEps(\hat\ell)=1\vdash$
    \[ 
     f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))) = f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))).
    \]
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
Indeed, we will prove that the LHS and the RHS of the equation are both identical to $g(\vec x)$.\\ 
    
    \noindent \textbf{(LHS).} Note that by a technical proposition unfolding the conditional non-$\eps$ form, we know that 
    \begin{align*}
    & f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))))) \\ 
    = & \begin{cases}
    g(\vec x) & \Or(\IsEps(\hat \ell'),\IsEps(y'')) \\ 
    h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR(y''))) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    where 
    \begin{align*}
    y''&\eqdef \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y')))), \\  
    \hat\ell'&\eqdef \ITRL(\ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, y'')).
    \end{align*}
    Note that we can prove $\EQL(\ITR(\ell :: u, y''), s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))))=1$ (details omitted), so that by a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$:
    \[
    \hat \ell' =\ITRL(\ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, y'')) = \ITRL(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))) = \hat\ell.
    \]
    Since $\IsEps(\hat\ell)=1$ is available in the antecedent, we can apply the rewrite rule $(\hat =_/)$, unfold $\Or$ and $\ITE$, and conclude that 
    \[
    f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))))) = g(\vec x). 
    \]

    \noindent \textbf{(RHS).} Again, by a technical proposition unfolding the conditional non-$\eps$ form, we know that 
    \begin{align*}
        & f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell, s_i(y')))) \\ 
    =   & \begin{cases}
        g(x) & \Or(\IsEps(\hat \ell'), \IsEps(y'')) \\ 
        h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell, \TR(y''))) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    where 
    \begin{align*}
    y''&\eqdef \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))), \\  
    \hat\ell'&\eqdef \ITRL(\ell, \ITR(\ell, y'')).
    \end{align*}
    Note that we can prove $\EQL(\ITR(\ell, y''),\ITR(\ell, s_i(y')))=1$ (details omitted), so that by a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$: 
    \[
    \hat\ell' = \ITRL(\ell, \ITR(\ell, y'')) = \ITRL(\ell,\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))) = \hat\ell. 
    \]
    Since $\IsEps(\hat\ell)=1$ is available in the antecedent, we can apply the rewrite rule $(\hat =_/)$, unfold $\Or$ and $\ITE$, and conclude that 
    \[
    f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell, s_i(y')))) = g(\vec x). 
    \] 
    This completes the proof.
</informal_proof>

<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). This chapter develops more advanced data structures (lists, tuples, finite functions) and reasoning principles (e.g.\ list induction, bounded comprehension, recursion on lists). $\IsList(\ell), \Len(\ell), \Tail, \Head$ are list primitives; $\ITRL(\ell, x)$ iteratively removes the rightmost $|x|$ elements of $\ell$. $\EQL(x,y)$ tests whether $x$ and $y$ have the same length. $\IMP(\PV)$ is an imperative programming language whose programs reduce to $\PV$ functions. Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Lemma (book label `lmm: tech ind list noneps case`).

$\PVPL$ proves $\Gamma,\IsEps(\hat\ell)=0\vdash$
    \[ 
    f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))) = f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))).
    \]
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
Similar to the proof of the $\eps$-case lemma for induction on lists, we can apply a technical proposition unfolding the conditional non-$\eps$ form to show that: 
    \begin{align*}
    & f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))))) \\ 
    = & \begin{cases}
    g(\vec x) & \Or(\IsEps(\hat \ell'),\IsEps(y'')) \\ 
    h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR(y''))) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    where it is provable that $\hat\ell'=\hat\ell$, and $y''\eqdef \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))$. It can be proved that $\IsEps(y'') = 0$ as $\IsEps(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ell))) = 0$. Therefore, by the assumption that $\IsEps(\hat\ell) = 0$, we can conclude by applying the rewrite rule and unfolding that: 
    \begin{align}
        &~f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, s_i(y'))))) \nonumber \\ 
    =   &~h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))))). \label{equ: tech shitty 1}
    \end{align}

    Similarly, we can also prove that 
    \begin{align}
        &~f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell, \ITR(\ell, s_i(y')))) \nonumber \\ 
    =   &~h(\vec x, u, \ell, f'(\vec x, \ell, \TR(\ITR(\ell,\ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))))). \label{equ: tech shitty 2}
    \end{align}
    Notice that the LHS of the equation `equ: tech shitty 1` and the equation `equ: tech shitty 2` are the LHS and RHS of the equation in the lemma, respectively. Therefore, it suffices to prove that 
    \begin{align}
        &~f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \TR(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))))) \nonumber \\
    =   &~f'(\vec x, \ell, \TR(\ITR(\ell,\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))). \label{equ: tech shitty goal}
    \end{align}

    Finally, notice that $\PV$ proves:
    \begin{align*}
    & \EQL(\TR(\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(y'))))),\ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, y')))) = 1, \\ 
    & \EQL(\TR(\ITR(\ell,\ITR(\ell,s_i(y')))), \ITR(\ell,\ITR(\ell,y'))) = 1.
    \end{align*}
    (The detail is omitted.) We can therefore modify our goal the equation `equ: tech shitty goal` using a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$ and the rewrite rule to: 
    \begin{align*}
        f'(\vec x, \ell :: u, \ITR(\ell :: u, s_0(\ITR(\ell, y')))) 
    =   f'(\vec x, \ell, \ITR(\ell,\ITR(\ell,y'))),
    \end{align*}
    which is available as the third bullet of the antecedent (see the definition of $\Gamma$ above).
</informal_proof>

<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in $\PV$ and $\PVPL$ (the predicate-logic extension of $\PV$). Background on $\PV/\PVPL$ is summarized in the glossary.

Proposition (book label `prop: tech properties prflist`).

The following assertions are provable in $\PVPL$:
    \begin{compactitem}
    \item $\IsList[\ell]\vdash \PrfList(\ell,\eps) = \eps$; 
    \item $\IsList[\ell]\vdash\IsList[\PrfList(\ell,x)]$
    % \item $\EQL(x,y) = 1\vdash \PrfList(\ell, x) = \PrfList(\ell, y)$. 
    \item $\IsList[\ell] \vdash \PrfList(\ell,x) = \PrfList(\ell,s_i(x))\lor \PrfList(\ell,x) = \Tail(\PrfList(\ell,s_i(x)))$. 
    \end{compactitem}
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
The first bullet is equivalent to $\ITRL(\ell,\ell) = \eps$, which has been proved in Step 1 of the proof of the theorem permitting recursive definitions over lists (see the section proving recursion on lists). 

The second bullet can be proved by induction on $y$ on the stronger statement $\IsList[\ell]\vdash \IsList[\ITRL(\ell,y)]$. The base case is trivial as $\ITRL(\ell,\eps) = \eps$, while the induction case follows from the definition equation of $\ITRL$ and $\IsList$. 

% The third bullet follows from the two assertions: $\EQL(x,y)=1\vdash \ITRL(\ell,x) = \ITRL(\ell, y)$ and $\vdash \EQL(\ITR(\ell,x),\ITR(\ell, y))=1$. Note that the former assertion has been proved in a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$, and the latter assertion can be easily proved by induction on $x$ and $y$ simultaneously using $(\Ind_2)$. 

For the last bullet, we first prove a case study on whether $\ITR(x,\ell) = \eps$. If this is not the case, we have that $\ITR(\ell,x) = \ITR(\ell,s_i(x)) = \eps$ and the left side of the disjunction holds by the reflexivity of equality. Otherwise, we know that 
\[ 
\PV\vdash \EQL(\ITR(\ell,x), s_0(\ITR(\ell,s_i(x)))) = 1.  
\] 
and it suffices to prove for a fresh variable $z$ that 
\[
\ITRL(\ell, z) = \ITRL(\ell, s_0(z)) \lor \ITRL(\ell, s_0(z)) = \Tail(\ITRL(\ell, z))
\]
by the second bullet of a technical proposition collecting properties of $\EQL$. The right side of the disjunction is implied by the definition equation of $\ITRL$.
</informal_proof>

<informal_theorem>
Setting: Working in $\PV$ (Cook's polynomial-time equational theory) and its predicate-logic extension $\PVPL$. We use Cook's translation $[\cdot]_\Cook$, which sends a $\PV$ equation $s(\vec x) = t(\vec x)$ on input lengths $\vec n = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ to a propositional formula $[s = t]_\Cook^{\vec n}$ over $\poly(\vec n)$ variables. Concretely, the translation introduces input variables for $\vec x$, internal variables encoding intermediate computation, output variables encoding $s(\vec x)$ and $t(\vec x)$, and a set $\Gamma$ of 3-clause-form constraints; the translation has the property that any assignment satisfying all of $\Gamma$ has the output variables equal to the value of the function at the input.

The propositional proof system used is $\EF$ (Extended Frege), with axiom schemes $\K, \S, \D$, the Modus Ponens rule, and an Extension rule "from a fresh variable $z$, deduce $z \leftrightarrow \varphi$". $\EF$ proofs are encoded in $\PV$ as lists of formulas; $\Verifier(\pi)$ is the $\PV$ predicate that checks whether $\pi$ is a syntactically valid $\EF$ proof, $\Conc(\pi) = \varphi$ extracts the conclusion, and $\Head$ extracts the last line of the proof list.

Lemma (Arithmetic-to-Propositional direction; first half of Cook's translation theorem) (book location `07-propositional-trans.tex:216`).

Let $s(\vec x) = t(\vec x)$ be a $\PV$ equation, where $\vec x = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Suppose that $\PV$ proves $s(\vec x) = t(\vec x)$. Then there exists a $\PV$ function $\Gen_{s=t}$ such that $\PVPL$ proves
\[
\ell = \Gen_{s=t}(z_1, \dots, z_k) \;\vdash\; \Verifier(\ell) = 1 \;\land\; \Conc(\Head(\ell)) = [s = t]_\Cook^{|z_1|, \dots, |z_k|}.
\]
That is, $\Gen_{s=t}$ produces, for every input-length vector $(|z_1|, \dots, |z_k|)$, a valid $\EF$ proof of the propositional translation $[s = t]_\Cook^{|z_1|, \dots, |z_k|}$.
</informal_theorem>

<informal_proof>
We sketch the proof; the construction of $\Gen_{s=t}$ can be extracted from the inductive argument below.

The argument is by induction on the $\PV$ proof of $s(\vec x) = t(\vec x)$, performed in the meta-theory: we translate the $\PV$ proof line-by-line into short $\EF$ proofs of the corresponding propositional translations. The induction hypothesis is that for the first $i-1$ lines of the $\PV$ proof, the propositional translation on every input-length vector $\vec m$ admits a $\poly(\vec m)$-size $\EF$ proof; we show that the $i$-th line also has this property.

There are three cases depending on what justifies the $i$-th line.

\textbf{Case 1: definition axioms.} Definition axioms of functions introduced by composition admit short $\EF$ proofs trivially (since the translation of a composition is the gate-by-gate composition of the translations of its parts). For functions $f(\vec x, y)$ introduced by limited recursion from $g(\vec x), h_0, h_1$ (with bound functions $k_0, k_1$ satisfying $\PV \vdash \ITR(h_i(\vec x, y, z), z \circ k_i(\vec x, y)) = \eps$), we must show that the translations of the recursion equations
\[
f(\vec x, \eps) = g(\vec x), \qquad f(\vec x, s_i(y)) = h_i(\vec x, y, f(\vec x, y))
\]
admit short $\EF$ proofs.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Base case $f(\vec x, \eps) = g(\vec x)$.} The translation of $f(\vec x, \eps)$ uses indicator variables $w_1, \dots, w_{n_y}$ for the input-length encoding of $y$; one proves in $\EF$ that $w_{n_y} = 1$ and $w_j = 0$ for $j \ne n_y$ (i.e.\ the input length is $0$). Under those assignments the internal variable $z_0^{n_y}$ that maintains the output of $g(\vec x)$ becomes the output, matching the right-hand side.
\item \emph{Recursion case $f(\vec x, s_i(y)) = h_i(\vec x, y, f(\vec x, y))$.} One first proves that the input-length encoding of $s_i(y)$ is shifted by $1$ from that of $y$: if $w_1, \dots, w_{n_y}$ are the LHS length variables and $w_1', \dots, w_{n_y}'$ are the RHS length variables, $w_j \leftrightarrow w_{j+1}'$. Then for each input length $j \in [n_y]$, the LHS and RHS perform the same computation, so their output variables are equal. Both steps reduce to the gate-by-gate equivalence task described below.
\end{itemize}

The recurring "gate-by-gate" subtask is: given two copies $C_1, C_2$ of the same circuit (encoded as 3-CNFs with extension variables) on inputs $x_1, x_2 \in \zo^n$, prove from $\Gamma = \{x_{1i} \leftrightarrow x_{2i} : i \in [n]\}$ that $C_1(x_1) \leftrightarrow C_2(x_2)$. This is done gate-by-gate: at each gate one only manipulates a 3-CNF of $O(1)$ size, which Frege can prove with $O(1)$ size, so the total size is bounded by the gate count.

\textbf{Case 2: logical rules (L0)–(L4).}
\begin{itemize}
\item (L0)–(L2) (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity) admit immediate short $\EF$ proofs from the induction hypothesis.
\item (L3) congruence. Given induction-hypothesis proofs of $s_1 = t_1, \dots, s_n = t_n$, the output variables of $s_j$ are propositionally equal to those of $t_j$. By the definition of the translation of compositions, the input variables of $f$ in $f(s_1, \dots, s_n)$ are identified with the output variables of the $s_j$'s (and similarly for the $t_j$'s). The remaining task is exactly the gate-by-gate circuit-equivalence task above, and is provable in polynomial size (without the extension rule).
\item (L4) substitution. The induction hypothesis gives proofs of the translation of $s = t$ on \emph{any} input-length vector. Let $\ell_v$ be the output length of the translation of $v$. Take the proof of $s = t$ where the input length of $x$ is $\ell_v$ and the other input lengths are chosen to match the lengths needed for $s[x/v] = t[x/v]$; identifying the input variables of $x$ with the output variables of $v$ yields the desired translation.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Case 3: structural induction.} Suppose $g(\vec x), h_0(\vec x, y, z), h_1(\vec x, y, z)$ are $\PV$ functions and $f_1(\vec x, y), f_2(\vec x, y)$ both satisfy
\[
f_j(\vec x, \eps) = g(\vec x), \qquad f_j(\vec x, s_i(y)) = h_i(\vec x, y, f_j(\vec x, y)) \quad (i \in \{0,1\},\, j \in \{1,2\}),
\]
and we want to derive $f_1(\vec x, y) = f_2(\vec x, y)$. We perform an inner induction on the input length of $y$ in the meta-theory. For each fixed input length $n_y$, we use intermediate variables $z_0, z_1, \dots, z_{n_y}$ to record the values of $f_2(\vec x, y_{\le j})$ at the prefixes of $y$, introduced by the extension rule; this is the only place where extension is essential, because we need polynomially many fresh variables to record the recursion trace.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Base ($j = 0$).} An $\EF$ proof of "$z_0$ encodes the output of $g(\vec x)$" comes from the induction hypothesis on the recursion axiom for $f_2$ at $\eps$; combined with the (already-available) $\EF$ proof that $g(\vec x)$ encodes $f_2(\vec x, \eps)$, transitivity gives an $\EF$ proof that $z_0$ encodes $f_2(\vec x, \eps)$.
\item \emph{Inductive step.} From the proof that $z_j$ encodes $f_2(\vec x, y_{\le j})$, we derive a proof that $z_{j+1}$ encodes $f_2(\vec x, y_{\le j+1})$ by translating the recursion axiom $f_2(\vec x, s_i(y_{\le j})) = h_i(\vec x, y_{\le j}, f_2(\vec x, y_{\le j}))$ at the appropriate input length; this again reduces to the gate-by-gate circuit-equivalence task.
\end{itemize}
The same argument applies to $f_1$, and the resulting proofs combine to give the translation of $f_1(\vec x, y) = f_2(\vec x, y)$ at every input length.

This exhausts the cases for inductive translation of a $\PV$ proof; combining them yields a $\PV$ function $\Gen_{s=t}$ that, on any input-length vector, outputs a polynomial-size $\EF$ proof of the propositional translation, as required.
</informal_proof>
